newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Plan to ban student politics divides Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Plan to ban student politics divides Bangladesh.

text.p: Bangladesh appeared divided on Monday over a presidential proposal for a temporary ban on student politics which has in the past triggered violence and even deaths on campuses.
"If national interest requires, so-called student politics should be suspended temporarily," the country's new President Shahabuddin Ahmed said on Sunday.

"Students have no fundamental right to do politics on the campus. They must realise that they are being used as instruments for getting political power," Ahmed, who took office last week, told politicians at the presidential palace.
The president said both the ruling and opposition parties should "delink" themselves from their respective student wings.
He was particularly worried about violence on the country's biggest campus, Dhaka University, a hotbed of politics since before the country's independence from Pakistan in 1971.
Officials records say at least 20 students have been killed in political battles at the 28,000-student university over the past five years.
Putting an end to student politics would not be easy, political analysts said on Monday.
Some teachers and students opposed the proposal.

Dr. Arefin Siddiqui, secretary-general of the Dhaka University Teachers' Association, said: "Banning student politics is no answer to...campus violence. What is needed is to delink student groups from political parties."

Jatiyatabadi Chattra Dal (JCD), the student wing of the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), opposed the president's proposal, saying it could be a "conspiracy by the ruling (Awami League) party to throttle political opponents".
But others said they supported the president's initiative to stamp out campus politics.
"A moratorium on student politics can be a way to get rid of violence...and restore academic atmosphere," said Professor A.K. Azad Chowdhury, vice-chancellor of Dhaka University.
